event.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup supply-chain attack on Microsoft 365 tenants
event.cvss: Not available in the research file.
event.affected: Managed Service Providers using ConnectWise Cloud Backup and their Microsoft 365 customers. Huntress saw unauthorized sign-ins in about 173 tenants; Microsoft reported attempts on more than 2,250 tenants.
event.attacker: Storm-0940, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence
event.status: Cloud Backup and related services were suspended while credentials were disabled and services restored in phases. Investigation continued.
event.summary: Attackers used a stolen ConnectWise Cloud Backup application credential to sign into customer Microsoft 365 tenants. ConnectWise shut down access on 17 October and revoked the application credentials. Microsoft later attributed the activity to Storm-0940. No backup data was reported stolen.

happened.p: ConnectWise Cloud Backup was a multi-tenant service used by managed service providers to back up Microsoft 365 data. The service had broad permissions in customer tenants, including access to mailboxes, files, Teams messages and directory data.

Attackers used the application identity rather than a user password. In at least one MSP tenant, a related ConnectWise Teams/Cloud Management app added itself as a Global Administrator and injected new client secrets into other trusted applications, which could have allowed access to persist after the original credential was revoked. Microsoft and ConnectWise did not identify a software vulnerability; the credential itself was the way in.

how.p: The attackers obtained the app credential, authenticated as the trusted service principal and requested Microsoft Graph access tokens. Because many tenants had already approved the app, the tokens carried the app permissions. The attackers could then read data or make changes without users' passwords.
A service principal is an application identity in Microsoft Entra ID. Its client secret acts like a password; an access token is the permission proof issued after authentication.

impact.p: The incident affected MSPs and Microsoft 365 tenants at scale. Public reporting described unauthorized sign-ins in at least 173 tenants and more than 2,250 targeted tenant IDs. Cloud Backup, SaaS Security and Cloud Management services were interrupted. ConnectWise said there was no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed, but tenant data and persistent application changes required review.

fix.p: ConnectWise disabled the affected application IDs, revoked certificates and kept services suspended while security reviews were completed. Partners were told to review audit logs, remove unexpected credentials and follow formal reconnection instructions. Existing backup archives were reported as encrypted and safe.

entry.text: Unauthorized service-principal sign-ins were observed across customer tenants.
ConnectWise announced an investigation and shared indicators for partners to check.
ConnectWise disabled affected application identities and revoked credentials, suspending the service.
Microsoft published attribution to Storm-0940 and described targeting at about 2,900 attempts per minute.
ConnectWise continued phased restoration and said encrypted backup archives remained safe.

lessons.lesson: A trusted vendor credential can become a cross-customer key.
Application permissions should be reviewed and limited, even when the app is legitimate.
Revoking the original credential is not enough if attackers create new credentials for persistence.
Tenant audit logs and service-principal activity need regular review.

glossary.term: An attack that reaches customers through a trusted vendor or service.
An application identity used to access cloud services.
A secret value an application uses like a password.
A short-lived proof that grants an application permissions.
The highest-privilege administrative role in a Microsoft 365 tenant.

event.title: eMudhra weak private keys in certificate authority certificates
event.affected: Eight intermediate certificate authorities: six for TLS and two for code signing. They were trusted by major browsers and operating systems. Domestic Indian DSC and eSign services were not affected.
event.attacker: No malicious attacker identified; the keys were weak by mistake
event.status: All eight intermediates were revoked and major browsers blocked them. eMudhra later exited the SSL/TLS certificate business.
event.summary: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys were generated with extremely small private values. Anyone could brute-force the values from the public certificates, which could have enabled forged TLS or code-signing certificates. Vendors rapidly revoked trust, and no confirmed malicious use was reported.

happened.p: A key-generation ceremony in April 2025 accidentally created a second, ultra-weak key pair. Each P-384 private key had a value under 256; one example had the value 4. That is far too little randomness for a cryptographic private key.

With a weak intermediate CA key, an attacker could sign a certificate for a website or software package that browsers would normally trust. The issue was a manufacturing error, not an external breach of eMudhra systems.

how.p: The failure was low entropy: the private key had only about eight bits of possible value. A person with the public certificate could try the few hundred possible values until one matched. The private key could then be used to sign a fake certificate.

Browser and operating-system vendors used revocation lists and trust-store updates. This removed trust in certificates signed by the affected keys. A forged certificate would let an attacker intercept HTTPS traffic to a site (a man-in-the-middle attack) or sign malicious software.

impact.p: No actual breach of eMudhra systems or theft of user data was reported. The main impact was loss of trust in the affected CA hierarchy and the need to replace certificates. One U.S. customer ecosystem was reported to have about 30,800 certificates under the impacted hierarchy.

fix.p: eMudhra revoked all eight intermediates. Chrome used CRLSet, Firefox used OneCRL, and Microsoft, Apple and Android updated trust decisions. Developers and administrators were told to update CA bundles and software that carries its own trust store.

entry.text: eMudhra generated keys for eight intermediate CAs inside hardware security modules.
A researcher alerted root-store maintainers. Chrome and Firefox blocked the affected TLS intermediates within hours.
eMudhra revoked all eight affected intermediate certificates.
Apple and Google/Android blocked the same CAs.
Microsoft updated its certificate trust lists.
CERT-In published an advisory describing the incident and mitigation.
eMudhra announced its exit from the global SSL/TLS certificate business.

lessons.lesson: Private keys need strong, tested randomness even inside hardware security modules.
Trust stores must update quickly when a CA key is compromised.
Independent monitoring and certificate transparency can catch unexpected certificates.
Reducing dependence on one certificate authority limits blast radius.

glossary.term: An entity that issues digital certificates to verify websites or software.
Randomness used to make cryptographic keys hard to guess.
A certificate authority certified by a root CA to issue certificates.
Marking a certificate as no longer trusted before it expires.
The list of certificate authorities a browser or system trusts.

event.title: PHP2Shell: critical PHP remote code execution flaws
event.cvss: CVSS approximately 9.2–9.8; Red Hat rated CVE-2026-109618 at 8.1
event.affected: Web servers running affected PHP versions, including Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi and embedded PHP devices. More than 5.1 million Internet-facing hosts were estimated at risk.
event.status: PHP released fixes on 2026-10-21. CISA added the CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog; investigations continued. CISA's KEV patch deadline was 2026-10-29.
event.summary: Two critical PHP bugs allowed unauthenticated attackers to execute commands on vulnerable web servers. Attack probes were observed on 17 October, before the public fixes on 21 October, so administrators had to patch, audit and check for web shells.

happened.p: CVE-2026-109618 involves an out-of-memory cleanup path that can follow corrupted internal data. CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw where stale request state can be reused. Both can lead to remote code execution as the web-server account.
The flaws were in PHP core, not in a particular website. Attackers sent carefully crafted web requests; they did not need a login or SQL injection.

how.p: For the out-of-memory bug, an attacker sends data that makes PHP exceed its memory limit at a specific point, confusing cleanup. For the use-after-free bug, one request leaves stale session or error state behind and a later request on the same PHP worker process reuses it. In both cases, arbitrary commands can run over the network.
Remote code execution means the attacker can run commands as the web process. A honeypot is a decoy system used to observe attacks.

impact.p: More than 5.1 million Internet-facing hosts were estimated to have vulnerable PHP. Reported consequences included web shells, stolen data and chained compromises of network appliances. The public research also recorded more than 77,000 exploit attempts against WordPress sites without confirmed infections in one dataset.

fix.p: Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or use a vendor-patched package. If patching is delayed, apply the documented temporary configuration mitigations, restart workers and audit logs and files for shells or unusual child processes. PHP 8.1 and earlier are unsupported and have no official patch.

entry.text: Security teams reportedly identified the two PHP RCE bugs during preliminary research.
AWS telemetry observed the first exploit probes.
The CVE identifiers began circulating online.
PHP released fixed versions and live exploitation was confirmed.
Honeypots recorded successful shell sessions on vulnerable servers.
CISA added both CVEs to the KEV catalog.

lessons.lesson: Patch immediately when a critical flaw is being exploited.
Inventory PHP in servers, containers and appliances, not only visible websites.
Use logs, honeypots and detection rules to find exploitation.
Configuration mitigations reduce risk but do not replace a patch.

event.title: TeamUpdraft / UpdraftCentral WordPress backdoor via stolen keys
event.cvss: Not available in the research file.
event.affected: TeamUpdraft customer data and WordPress sites using UpdraftPlus with an active UpdraftCentral key. UpdraftPlus had more than 4 million installations; reports observed many malicious plugins.
event.status: The breach was contained. Updates revoked keys, but users still had to remove old keys and inspect sites for backdoors.
event.summary: Attackers accessed TeamUpdraft’s customer database, stole UpdraftCentral connection keys and used them to send trusted commands to connected WordPress sites. Malicious plugins created hidden administrator accounts and backdoors.

happened.p: UpdraftCentral lets one dashboard control backups and updates across many WordPress sites. A private connection key stored by the service authenticates remote commands.

After stealing those keys, attackers uploaded and activated malicious plugins. The plugins hid themselves and created administrator accounts, so disabling the service alone did not remove every implant.

how.p: The stolen private keys let attackers issue commands that looked authorized. One command uploaded a plugin archive. The plugin created a hidden admin user and could bypass normal login checks, giving attackers persistence even after key revocation.
A connection key is a secret digital code used to authenticate a remote command. A backdoor is hidden software that provides secret access.

impact.p: The customer database contained names, addresses, order history, hashed passwords, two-factor settings and connection keys. WordPress sites could be fully taken over. Reports observed more than 99 distinct malicious plugin names, while the exact number of compromised sites remained unknown. TeamUpdraft did not store payment card data, and backups stored by users in Google Drive, Dropbox or similar services were not directly compromised.

fix.p: Update UpdraftPlus to 1.26.13 or later (1.26.12/2.26.12 was the first revocation release; 1.26.13 corrected the revocation), remove old UpdraftCentral keys, rotate passwords and two-factor settings, and inspect plugins, files, administrator accounts and logs. Wordfence also released an emergency firewall rule. Updating alone did not remove already-installed backdoors.

entry.text: TeamUpdraft detected unauthorized access and attackers likely extracted customer data and connection keys.
The first malicious plugin installation was observed.
TeamUpdraft disclosed the incident and released updates that revoked old keys.
The breach was reported as contained and Wordfence released firewall rules.
The official incident page was updated with further findings.

lessons.lesson: Remote-management keys are as sensitive as passwords.
Connected services need regular audits and least privilege.
Revoke keys and investigate systems after a breach; do not assume revocation removes implants.
Unexpected plugins and administrator accounts are useful indicators.

event.title: ARTEX: AI-agent driven intrusion campaign
event.cvss: Not available in the research file.
event.affected: More than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, including government, defense, telecom and semiconductor organizations. About 140 targets were sensitive and at least 9 organizations had confirmed intrusions.
event.status: The campaign appeared complete and ARTEX was taken offline by its developer. Security firms published detection rules and mitigation guidance.
event.summary: Starting on 17 October, VAPOR PANDA used the ARTEX AI toolkit to scan hundreds of networks and breach at least nine of them at machine speed. The campaign targeted more than 200 organizations in 11 days and installed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor in the confirmed intrusions.

happened.p: ARTEX is an agentic penetration-testing framework powered by large language models. A human operator provided target scopes, then planner and worker agents scanned networks, selected exploits and carried out post-exploitation steps.

The agents installed BLOODALCHEMY, harvested administrator passwords and BitLocker keys, used a four-year-old email-server key to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes, and found VPN configuration files in an old email to move laterally. A human remained in the loop and issued instructions at critical points.

how.p: ARTEX scanned target ranges, used an LLM to interpret findings, selected or generated exploits and installed a backdoor after access. It also searched for credentials in directory attributes and old files, then used those secrets for lateral movement. Human instructions could redirect agents away from protected systems.
The attack was not a new vulnerability. It combined automation with existing weaknesses, poor credential hygiene and exposed services.

impact.p: More than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries were targeted, including sensitive government and corporate systems. At least 9 organizations had confirmed intrusions. The campaign exposed administrator passwords, disk-encryption keys, email and network configuration data, raising the speed and scale of cyber-espionage.

fix.p: Rotate signing keys, tokens, service credentials and old passwords. Enforce SAML validation and AWS IMDSv2, patch internet-facing systems, deploy endpoint detection on all servers, monitor high-volume scripted activity and apply the published ARTEX/BLOODALCHEMY detection rules.

entry.text: CrowdStrike observed the AI-driven intrusion campaign begin.
The approximately 11-day campaign concluded after targeting more than 200 organizations.
CrowdStrike published its report on ARTEX and VAPOR PANDA.
Further analysis described the scale and technical behavior.
Reports said the ARTEX developer took the framework offline and made it closed-source.
Defenders continued to rotate credentials and deploy detection rules.

lessons.lesson: AI increases attack speed and scale, so defenders must watch for automation.
Old keys and credentials become attack paths if they are not rotated.
High request volumes and scripted activity can reveal agentic attacks.
Human oversight remains important, but defense-in-depth is still required.

event.title: LiteLLM supply-chain attack
event.cvss: Not available in the research file.
event.affected: Any environment that installed LiteLLM v1.107.0 while the malicious release was available: developer laptops, CI pipelines and cloud AI gateways. LiteLLM had about 23 million weekly downloads. Enterprise/private LiteLLM releases were not affected.
event.attacker: Unknown; stolen GitHub CLI tokens were used
event.status: The malicious package and images were removed. Users were told to downgrade to v1.106.2 or earlier, delete startup-hook files, rotate secrets and rebuild affected environments.
event.summary: Attackers hijacked LiteLLM’s release pipeline and published a backdoored v1.107.0 to PyPI and Docker. Hidden Python startup files collected cloud credentials, developer keys, browser passwords and other secrets whenever Python ran.

happened.p: Attackers used stolen GitHub tokens from LiteLLM developers to redirect a release workflow to a lookalike fork. A one-line build change caused cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py to ship in the package.

Python automatically loads some .pth and sitecustomize files at interpreter startup. The payload used that behavior to steal AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Docker, SSH/GPG, browser and AI-provider secrets.

how.p: Stolen developer tokens allowed the attackers to run the release process. The malicious fork added files that execute automatically when Python starts, even if the user did not explicitly import LiteLLM. The code gathered secrets and sent them to attacker infrastructure.
This was a supply-chain attack because the build and distribution path was compromised, not because LiteLLM users installed a normal software bug.

impact.p: The package had about 49,000 downloads before removal, within a project with about 23 million weekly downloads. The malicious wheels were available for only about two hours, from roughly 11:40 to 13:23 UTC. Any affected environment could have exposed cloud accounts, developer resources, AI service credentials or enterprise data. No specific downstream breach was confirmed in the supplied research.

fix.p: Remove v1.107.0, pin to v1.106.2 or earlier, delete cook.pth, cook.py and sitecustomize.py, rotate all potentially exposed credentials, audit logs and rebuild affected environments from a clean state.

entry.text: Compromised LiteLLM v1.107.0 was published to PyPI.
Docker images for v1.107.0 and moving tags were built from the malicious fork.
PyPI quarantined the release and removed the wheels.
Docker tags were repointed or disabled.
LiteLLM resumed clean releases and removed the v1.107.0 tag.

lessons.lesson: Developer and CI tokens are high-value secrets.
Release workflows should accept only approved repositories and branches.
Pin and verify dependencies and container images.
Scan for unexpected interpreter startup files after a supply-chain incident.

event.title: Drupal Field UI & Entity List remote code execution patches
event.shortTitle: Drupal Field UI & Entity List RCE
event.affected: Drupal sites running vulnerable versions. About 151,000 Drupal sites (28.5% of reporting sites) were estimated to run vulnerable versions before the fix. CVE-2026-108097 affects Drupal core Field UI; CVE-2026-108099 affects the Entity List contributed module.
event.status: Drupal released security advisories and patches on 2026-10-14. Administrators were told to update core and the Entity List module and review logs. No confirmed exploitation in the wild was reported as of 2026-11-10.
event.summary: Drupal issued urgent patches for two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities: one in core Field UI and one in the contributed Entity List module. Core alone did not expose the Field UI flaw; a specific module combination had to be present. At least one attack path required no login. No confirmed exploitation in the wild was reported as of 10 November 2026.

happened.p: CVE-2026-108097 is in Drupal core's Field UI code, but on its own core did not expose it. It was only reachable when certain contributed modules passed requests into that code. CVE-2026-108099 is in the Entity List contributed module. In at least one attack path no login was required, so any visitor could trigger it.

Drupal published advisories SA-CORE-2026-014 and SA-CONTRIB-2026-218 on 14 October 2026, with patches the same day. Until sites updated, the advisory suggested uninstalling the core field_ui module as a temporary workaround.

how.p: A contributed module accepts a crafted request and passes the input into Drupal's Field UI or Entity List code path. A logic bug there causes Drupal to execute part of that input as code, so the attacker's code runs with the web server account's permissions.

The research describes this chain but reports no confirmed exploitation in the wild. The risk is highest where multiple contributed modules are installed and content endpoints are exposed to unauthenticated visitors.

impact.p: A successful exploit could change site content, read server-side data, install a backdoor or pivot to other systems. About 151,000 sites were estimated to be running vulnerable versions before patching, from one research estimate. No confirmed exploitation in the wild was reported as of 10 November 2026, so the main impact was urgent exposure and patch work.

fix.p: Update Drupal core to 10.6.19, 11.3.19 or 11.4.10 and the Entity List module to 3.0.10. If updating is delayed, uninstall the core field_ui module. Drupal Steward virtual patching may block some attacks but is not guaranteed to cover every exploit path. Review access and error logs and investigate unexpected files or administrator activity afterwards.

entry.text: Drupal issued a public service announcement scheduling a critical security release for 14 October.
Drupal published SA-CORE-2026-014 and SA-CONTRIB-2026-218 with patches for the Field UI and Entity List flaws.
SecurityWeek, GBHackers and other outlets summarised the advisories, warned of fast exploitation risk and urged immediate updates.
No confirmed exploitation in the wild had been reported; administrators were expected to have applied the updates.

lessons.lesson: A security release is only protective after it is installed.
CMS inventories must include contributed modules, not only core.
Review logs after a critical web vulnerability is disclosed.
Least privilege limits what a compromised web process can do.
